The FullerThaler Behavioral Growth ETF (NASDAQ:FTG) is a brand-new vehicle asking investors to bet that other investors are wrong. FTG, which lists on Nasdaq under a prospectus dated July 30, 2026, applies Fuller & Thaler's behavioral-finance framework to growth equities, screening for names where the manager believes the market has overreacted to news. With only 16 trading days of history and a last price of $23.22, FTG has no track record to speak of, and that is precisely the problem worth framing for anyone considering the fund.

Rawpixel.com / Shutterstock.com

Behavioral factor strategies are designed to pay off across full market cycles. They can trail badly during narrow, momentum-led markets, and a few months of live returns prove nothing in either direction. FTG's one-month return of -4.72% against QQQ at -1.69% and IWO at -5.37% is a data point, not a verdict.

Fund Basics and the Fee Hurdle

FTG carries a gross expense ratio of 1.35% and a net expense ratio of 0.79% after a fee waiver. That net figure is high for a US equity ETF, and the gap between gross and net matters: if the adviser lets the waiver expire, roughly 56 basis points of annual return would evaporate. AUM figures are not yet disclosed in the fund's public data, and no NPORT holdings snapshots are on file. Investors should treat both as monitoring items rather than known quantities.

Intel stock climbed earlier in the week after an unconfirmed report that the company could raise selected PC processor prices by 10%. That report isn't confirmed Intel policy, and today's fade suggests some holders are ringing the register while the fundamentals stay unchanged.
